coverage.note: Corrections come from the full audit of 2026-09-26: two independent readers per lesson, a third settling disagreements, reconciled with the 2026-09-24 hand sweep (a hand check of 20 scored rows found 17 right). 678 fixes Amal voiced or typed, filed in an approved rule, are counted. Uses are machine-counted: every time his Arabic exercises the rule, right or wrong; a fix with no counted use within 2 s counts as a use too, so a rule never has more mistakes than uses. Unscored = no counter sees his right uses of the rule, so its fixes are listed but no % is given. Asks: his own questions about a form (rule M1). Untested = he never used it in any recorded lesson, or it is a sound (F). Not taught yet = Amal has not taught the rule (her notes, 2026-09-27): no score, left out of every total. 19 corrections are shown but not counted (Amal's notes: not taught yet, or not a mistake - list in data/amal-grammar-notes-2026-09-29.json). A score built from a lesson that is not verified yet is marked with ≈ (hover or tap it for why).

audit.method: Amal re-says one of Medi's words in another shape (voice within 25s, or typed in the Meet chat), or names the rule in English. Words are compared across Arabic script, Latin and Arabizi. Scored against a hand-labelled gold set (docs/data/grammar-goldset.json). Never guessed: UNFILED when no rule fits.

rules.name: el- (the)
rules.one_line: `el-` marks a thing you already know; nothing marks a new one.
rules.why: English has 'a' and 'the'. Arabic only has 'the' - leaving it off is how you say 'a'.
more: "el" is used for general nouns: el-tuffaa7 zaaki = apples are delicious; el-shita baared = winter is cold. (Amal)
Sun and moon letters: no need. Not a priority - do NOT mark it as an error if he doesn't use them correctly. (Amal)
So a sun/moon-letter slip (el-shams vs esh-shams) is never scored. Only el- there / not there counts.

rules.name: idafa (possession)
rules.one_line: Thing first, owner second - and the first word never takes `el-`.
rules.why: There is no word for 'of'. You just put the two nouns next to each other.
more: el-bait Medi is always wrong - the first noun drops el-.
The LAST noun decides whether the whole phrase is definite.
bait m3allem = a teacher's house.  bait el-m3allem = the teacher's house.
If a noun ends with a possessive pronoun it's definite and doesn't take "el": bait u5ti = my sister's house; bent u5t jaarti = my neighbor's niece. (Amal)

rules.name: possessive endings
rules.one_line: Stick the owner on the end of the word.
rules.why: Instead of 'my name', Arabic says 'name-my' as one word.
more: The set: -i my, -ak your (m), -ek your (f), -o his, -ha her, -na our, -kom your (pl), -hom their.
baiti my house, baitha her house, baithom their house.
Biddi and 3indi conjugate with possessive endings (they are not real verbs): biddo = he wants, 3indna = we have. (Amal)
After a vowel: -ak -> -k, -ek -> -ki, -o -> long vowel + h: kursik = your (m) chair, awa3iki = your (f) clothes, abuh = his father. (Amal)
Possessive endings also give object pronouns on verbs, except "me" is -ni: a3tini = give me, a3tih = give him. (Amal)
Dual -ain words: eed -> eedayy, eedaik, eedaiki, eedaikom, eedaih, eedaiha, eedaina, eedaihom. (Amal)
ijer -> ijrayy, ijraik, ijraiki, ijraikom, ijraih, ijraiha, ijraihom, ijraina. (Amal)
daan/denain -> dinayy, dinaik, dinaiki, dinaikom, dinaih, dinaiha, dinahom, dinaina. (Amal)
7awalain -> 7awalayy, 7awalaik, 7awalaiki, 7awalaikom, 7awalaih, 7awalaiha, 7awalaihom, 7awalaina. (Amal)
Not every dual works like this (no "youmayy"); the list grows as he learns more. (Amal)

rules.name: plurals
rules.one_line: Some add an ending, many change shape, and two has its own form.
rules.why: Arabic has three plurals: regular endings, irregular reshapes, and a special 'exactly two'.
more: Regular: -een (people, m) and -aat (things/f) - muwazzaf -> muwazzafeen.
Irregular: you memorise them - bait->byoot, bab->bwaab, shubbak->shababeek.
Exactly two: add -ein - yom->yomein, saa3a->saa3tain.

rules.name: demonstrative keeps el-
rules.one_line: The noun after hada / hadi / hadol keeps its `el-`.

Superlatives are the exception - they never take el-: hadi a2al akleh.

rules.name: b-drop after modals
rules.one_line: A verb followed by another verb: the second one loses its b-. Same after want/must/can words.
rules.why: The first word already carries the tense, so the second verb goes bare.
more: The real rule: if a verb is followed by another verb, the second loses the b. (Amal)
Also after modal words: biddi, laazem, mumken, jaay 3abali. (Amal)
Also after a statement like it's nice / it's important / most likely: muhem te3raf = it's important to know; 3ala el-a8lab niji = we'll most likely come. (Amal)
Verb + verb: ba7eb, ba2dar, baballesh, bajarreb + a bare verb.
laazem aru7 I have to go - never laazem baru7.

rules.name: kaan + verb = used to / was doing
rules.one_line: kaan + a present verb: something you used to do, or were doing (past continuous).
rules.why: kaan plus a present verb puts it in the past: over and over back then, or going on at that moment.
more: Also means past continuous: kunet aqra2 = I was reading; kaanat tetbu5 = she was cooking. (Amal)
The b- after kaan: some verbs keep it, some drop it. It is NOT a rule - b- kept or dropped after kaan is never marked wrong. (Amal)
kaan bishrab ahwe kul yom he used to drink coffee every day.
kaan laazem goes with this too: kaan laazem + past = should have; kaan laazem + present = should have OR had to. Amal advises using it with the present. Scored under B16. (Amal)
Taught in lessons: Amal corrected this 1 time(s) out loud (09-24 sweep). No longer a gap rule - scored (Medi 2026-09-25).

rules.name: bakoon / ykoon
rules.one_line: No 'to be' in the plain present - but bikoon comes in for habits, for biddi/3indi in the past and future, and to mean 'probably'.
rules.why: This is the 'being' verb that appears only in certain slots.
more: Plain now: drop it - ana ta3baan.
Habitual with usually / sometimes / every: 3aadatan bikoon mash8ool 3ala el-wa7de = he's usually busy at 1:00. (Amal)
With biddi / 3indi in the past and future it is REQUIRED: kaan biddi = I wanted; ra7 ykoon 3indi = He will have. (Amal)
With lamma / iza: lamma ykoon biddak = when you want; iza bikoon 3indak = if you have. Here it is NOT strict - leaving it out after lamma / iza is not marked wrong. (Amal)
Bikoon can also mean "probably": bikoon m3asseb halla = he's probably angry now; bitkoon teshte8el = she's probably working. (Amal; her Doc's autocorrect wrote "Bitcoin teshte8el")
To check with Amal: she glossed ra7 ykoon 3indi as "He will have"; ykoon 3indi reads as "I will have".

baz3al I get sad -> baza33el I make someone sad.
bazha2 I get bored -> bazahhe2 I bore people.

rules.name: 3am = right now

rules.name: verb matches its subject
rules.one_line: The verb's person, gender and number must match who or what is doing it.
examples: the company that sells it washes it (sharika is feminine -> bet-)
what excites you? (one thing -> singular verb)
rules.why: English verbs barely change ('I/you/they sell'). Arabic verbs change for every person: a feminine noun takes the she-form, a plural takes -u, 'I' takes a-/ba-.
more: Present tense: the prefix/ending must be the right person - bey3asseb-ni (it annoys me), not ba3asseb-ni; testa3mel (she uses), not testa3meli.
A noun subject decides the form: the cup enkasarat (feminine), meetings bey-zah2u-ni (plural).
Past-tense endings for ana/inta/hiyye stay in B5; adjectives stay in A8.
Found 26 times in the 2026-09-24 sweep of all 13 lessons. Added by Medi 2026-09-25.

rules.name: illi
rules.one_line: 'the one that' - never changes shape. No el-, no illi.
examples: the thing I like the most
there is a song that I know
rules.why: One word covers that / which / who, for everything - but only after a definite word.
more: No el, no illi: if the word before illi is not definite (no el- and no possessive ending), don't add illi. (Amal)
aktar ishi ba7ebbo = the thing I like the most; seyyarti illi basoo2ha = my car that I drive; fi u8niyye ba3rafha = there is a song that I know. (Amal)
It never changes for gender or number.
The clause after it usually needs the C2 pointer ending - ishtareto not ishtarait.

candidates.why: After the definite noun the clause needs إلي; after Amal's 'That I make' he said إلي بعمله.
After the indefinite يوم واحد no connector is used; she said 'No إنه' (and 'No اللي' when he tried اللي).

rules.name: question words
rules.one_line: The basic set.
rules.why: Arabic doesn't need a 'do' helper - the question word just goes first.
more: shu what, wein where, keef how, 2adaish how much, kam how many, lesh why, meen who, aymta when.

kam always takes the singular: kam dars = how many lessons. (Amal) See E5.
kam also means few: 3indi kam ishi = I have a few things. (Amal)

rules.name: preposition keeps el-
rules.one_line: Where English drops 'the', Levantine keeps it.
rules.why: English says 'from home' and 'by car' with no 'the'. Arabic puts it back.
more: bi / la / fi fuse with it: bi-l..., la-l..., fi-l...
min / 3ala / ma3 keep it separate: min el-bait, 3ala el-6aawle.
No el- on a name (la-Mehdi, fi America), on something already owned (ma3i, ma3 sadiqi), or when it really is indefinite (ma3 3aseer).

rules.name: endings on prepositions
rules.one_line: Stick the person on the end of the preposition. All take endings except bi.

ma3i with me, ma3ak with you, ma3o with him.
minni from me, minnak from you, minno from him.

la- has its own endings: ili, ilak, ilek, ilkom, ilo, ilha, ilhom, ilna. (Amal)

rules.one_line: Sounds English doesn't have - scored as pronunciation, not grammar.
rules.why: Dropping them makes a different word, or no word at all.
more: 2 = hamza glottal stop, 3 = ayn, 7 = ha, 5 = kha, 6 = ta, 8 = ghayn, 9 = sad.
Your recorded slips are mostly ayn, ta and ghayn.
rules.tally_title: Sounds ع ط غ ه (dropped or swapped)

rules.name: vowel length
rules.one_line: Holding a vowel longer changes the word.
rules.why: Arabic treats a long vowel and a short one as two different letters.
more: Written Arabic doesn't mark short vowels, so this can only be judged by ear.
In Arabizi a doubled letter means hold it: saam vs sam.

rules.name: causative verbs: 3 forms
rules.one_line: One root, two sides - doing it to someone vs it happening to you - made 3 ways: doubled middle, n-, or t-.
rules.why: Amal: this card explains causative verbs instead of shadda. The doubled middle letter is one of the three forms.
more: Doubled middle, then t- for the 'it happens to me' side: ba3allem teach -> bat3allam learn; ba8ayyer change -> bat8ayyar be changed. (Amal)
n- for the 'it happens to me' side: baz3ej annoy -> banze3ej be annoyed. (Amal)
Replaces the old shadda card (Amal 2026-09-30). make-X / get-X slips are scored under B12; this card is still not scored on its own (family F).
